case_study_insert.main_stem: Pinecrest Home Services (PHS) is a private limited company in the consumer services sector, providing domestic cleaning and maintenance visits and employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2015 by Aisha Pine, it operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. PHS plans to invest $480,000 in electric service vans and a mobile booking app, financed by $280,000 hire purchase and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $20 a unit and a selling price of $70, and currently produces 10,000 units a year, each a standard home visit. PHS faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and customer complaints about missed bookings are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Marketing and Operations Extract — Q3 2025: PHS completed 2,400 home visits last quarter with a first-time-fix rate of 91%, down from 95% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 33 to 52 per month. Average booking-to-visit time is 4.6 days. A survey of 380 households found that 66% would pay $9 more for eco-friendly cleaning, and 58% rebook based on punctuality. Records show 10 of 32 cleaners have not finished on-the-job training on the new booking app; certification courses cost $500 per cleaner.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Pinecrest Home Services for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.5% to 4.1%, increasing hire-purchase costs for business vehicles. (2) The national minimum wage rose by 7.0% from $12.80 to $13.70 per hour from April 2026. (3) Fuel and cleaning-product input costs rose 10.5% and consumer spending on home services grew 2.2%, while household income fell 1.4%.

questions.question_text: PHS plans to fund part of its $480,000 expansion with $280,000 hire purchase. Explain two advantages for PHS of using retained profit instead of hire purchase.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit of $200,000 needs no deposit, interest or monthly instalments, unlike the $280,000 hire-purchase agreement on the electric vans. With contribution of $50 on each $70 home visit, money not paid in hire-purchase charges can cover the $240,000 fixed costs and absorb the 10.5% rise in fuel and cleaning-product costs, protecting PHS's flat-structure cash flow.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps ownership of the vans and app with Aisha Pine from day one, whereas under hire purchase the lender owns the assets until the final payment and can repossess them if instalments are missed. Using internal funds avoids that risk on the vehicles central to 10,000 visits a year, and adds no interest payable beyond the $30,000 shown in Appendix 2, keeping the service competitive on the $70 price.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PHS's financing choice and home-visit economics.

questions.question_text: PHS is promoting its electric-van service and booking app. Consider local newspaper advertisements, customer referral incentives, or social media marketing. Which should PHS choose to win household customers? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper advertisements: Print reaches households in PHS's immediate service area and can carry a coupon for a first $70 visit. It is cheap per insertion but has a short reading life and cannot show the booking app or the eco-friendly message; much of the readership will not need cleaning, so it wastes part of the promotion budget needed alongside the $480,000 expansion.

Customer referral incentives: Offering existing clients a discount for introducing neighbours uses trusted word of mouth and suits a service where 58% of customers rebook on punctuality. It is low cost and builds loyalty, but growth is slow and depends on the current customer base; with 52 monthly complaints and a 91% first-time-fix rate, PHS risks spreading dissatisfaction if unhappy clients refer others, so referrals alone cannot fix the booking problem.

Social media marketing: Targeted local ads can reach exactly the households in PHS's service area and speak to the 66% of 380 surveyed who would pay $9 more for eco-friendly cleaning. Posts can demonstrate the app, the electric vans and punctuality, and can be measured by bookings. It takes time to build trust and needs honest, consistent content, but cost per booked visit is low and campaigns can be scaled as new vans arrive.

Recommendation: PHS should choose social media marketing. It targets households precisely, carries the eco-friendly message the survey supports and scales with the new vans. Newspaper advertisements are rejected as untargeted and forgettable, and referral incentives are rejected as too slow and risky while complaints are high; PHS can add a modest referral bonus later once punctuality recovers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited identification of the promotional options with minimal reference to PHS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to PHS and partial judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in PHS's context with a justified recommendation explaining why newspapers and referrals are rejected.

questions.question_text: PHS's labour turnover has reached 14% and complaints about missed bookings are rising. Explain two benefits for PHS of using team working to reduce turnover and improve reliability.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working lets PHS's 32 cleaners cover visits collectively when staff leave, so a 14% turnover rate does not automatically become a missed booking. Teams can share routes and app updates, reducing the 4.6-day booking-to-visit time and tackling the rise in complaints from 33 to 52 per month, which in turn protects the 10,000 visits a year needed to justify the $480,000 investment.

Point 2: Working in teams spreads knowledge of the new booking app and lifts the 91% first-time-fix rate, since colleagues can check each other's job records. Greater involvement and social contact raise commitment, lowering the 14% turnover and the cost of repeatedly recruiting; this matters because 10 of 32 cleaners still need app training and further churn would make that gap permanent.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to PHS's turnover, complaints and quality data.

questions.question_text: PHS must train 10 cleaners on the new booking app. Consider on-the-job training or certification courses at $500 per cleaner. Which should PHS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training on real visits teaches PHS's own app and route routines, costs no fees and keeps the 10 cleaners earning while they learn, protecting the 2,400 home visits completed last quarter. Experienced cleaners can mentor the 10 of 32 who are untrained, and the training can be fitted around the 4.6-day booking time. The weaknesses are that trainers are working cleaners whose own visits slow down, errors can be copied, and there is no formal certificate for customers who judge reliability.

Certification courses: At $500 per cleaner, certifying 10 staff costs $5,000 (10 × $500), small beside the $480,000 van and app investment. A recognised certificate could support the eco-friendly, professional image behind the 66% survey result and reassure households. However, 10 of a 32-strong workforce would be off the road during training, worsening missed bookings and the 52 monthly complaints, and generic course content may not match PHS's exact app, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: PHS should choose on-the-job training for all 10 cleaners, with a short certification course for one team leader. On-the-job training is cheaper, app-specific and avoids losing visit capacity while complaints are rising; full certification is rejected because $5,000 and 10 cleaners off the road would harm punctuality, the very thing 58% of customers rebook on.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited reference to PHS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods applied to PHS, including cost and service disruption.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Full evaluation of both methods in PHS's context with a justified decision that rejects full external certification and explains the cost and capacity trade-off.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PHS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($70 − $20) = $240,000 ÷ $50 = 4,800 units. Answer: break-even output is 4,800 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $70 − $20 = $50. Answer: contribution per unit is $50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PHS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 4,800-unit break-even output with 10,000 visits actually made: the margin of safety is 5,200 visits, showing the electric-van expansion can succeed even if demand dips.
2. Use the $50 contribution on a $70 visit to test pricing: 66% of 380 households would pay $9 more for eco-friendly cleaning, so managers can weigh a premium against losing bookings.
3. Check that 4,800 break-even visits produce enough contribution to meet the $280,000 hire-purchase commitment before adding more vans.
4. Monitor unit cost of $44 per visit ($240,000 ÷ 10,000 = $24 fixed plus $20 variable) to control 10.5% fuel cost inflation and to investigate the fall from a 95% to a 91% first-time-fix rate that drives 52 monthly complaints.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 4,800 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 5,200 against 10,000 visits; pricing using the $9 eco premium; meeting the $280,000 hire-purchase commitment; and unit-cost benchmarking at $44 to tackle the 91% fix rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PHS's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has PHS's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 14.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue grew from $960,000 to $1,100,000 while cost of sales rose from $576,000 to $616,000, so gross profit increased from $384,000 to $484,000. Gross profit as a share of revenue therefore improved from 40.0% to 44.0%. Operating profit rose from $96,000 to $154,000, so operating profit as a share of revenue went from 10.0% to 14.0%. Capital employed increased from $800,000 to $1,100,000, giving a return on capital of 12.0% in 2024 and 14.0% in 2025.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, and the largest gain is in the share of revenue left after direct visit costs, suggesting better control of fuel and labour per job as the van fleet expanded. The operating result also strengthened, helped by spreading $240,000 of fixed costs over more visits. However, finance lease payments rose from $20,000 to $30,000, and capital employed grew by $300,000 while operating profit grew by $58,000, so return on capital improved only modestly. The fall in first-time-fix rate from 95% to 91% and 14% turnover could erase these gains if reliability keeps slipping, and the extract gives no detail on lease maturities.

Conclusion: PHS's financial performance has improved. Gross profit as a share of revenue rose from 40.0% to 44.0%, operating profit as a share of revenue from 10.0% to 14.0%, and return on capital from 12.0% to 14.0%. All three measures point upward together, so the improvement is real, though higher lease payments and a narrow rise in return on capital mean management should watch the reliability data as the new vans bed in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or directional changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs and capital employed and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PHS of switching to eco-friendly cleaning products.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco products fit clear customer demand. PHS's survey found 66% of 380 households would pay $9 more for eco-friendly cleaning and 58% rebook on punctuality, so a green premium can lift revenue above the $70 price per visit and defend the $50 contribution as 10.5% input costs rise. It also supports the $480,000 electric-van investment by giving the fleet a consistent green brand.

Disadvantage: Eco-friendly products usually cost more than standard supplies, which would increase the $20 variable cost per visit or push the $240,000 fixed costs higher. With labour turnover at 14% and 10 of 32 cleaners still untrained on the booking app, PHS may deliver the green promise inconsistently, and any fall in the 91% first-time-fix rate would worsen the 52 monthly complaints.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PHS's survey, costs and staffing.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.1%, the 7.0% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in fuel and cleaning-product costs will affect PHS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise (3.5% to 4.1%): Hire-purchase costs on the electric vans are likely to be sensitive to rates. If the $280,000 hire-purchase agreement tracks the base rate, the 0.6 percentage-point increase adds 0.6% × $280,000 = $1,680 a year at most. That is small against $240,000 of fixed costs, and some agreements are fixed at the outset, in which case there is no extra charge. Higher rates may also reduce household spending, but the direct cash effect on PHS is modest.

Minimum wage increase (7.0%, to $13.70 an hour): PHS employs a workforce of 32, and cleaning roles are commonly hourly-paid, so this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual rates, so an honest annual total cannot be calculated. The defensible check is productivity: 10,000 visits across 32 staff is 312.5 visits per employee, so the rise is absorbable only if that productivity holds; otherwise unit labour cost lifts the $44 unit cost and narrows the $50 contribution per visit.

Fuel and cleaning-product inflation (10.5%): The $20 variable cost per visit is not decomposed in the insert, so only a labelled illustrative upper bound is honest. If the whole $20 were exposed, 10.5% × $20 = $2.10 extra per visit, and across 10,000 visits that is $21,000 a year (10,000 × $2.10), cutting contribution from $50 toward $47.90. PHS can recover part of this through the $9 eco premium accepted by 66% of surveyed households.

Conclusion: The 10.5% rise in fuel and cleaning-product costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 10,000 visits and directly erodes the $50 contribution that supports the $480,000 van and app programme, and no loan renegotiation can remove it. The wage rise is second but cannot be quantified from the insert, while the rate rise adds at most $1,680 a year and is clearly the smallest of the three changes.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to PHS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on PHS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in PHS's context with a justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
